title: Sebastian
synopsis: You're a young writer in London with a novel that won't sell. To finish it, you start escorting under a name that isn't yours. You promise yourself you can write your way back out.

nodes.text: You set up the profile under 'Sebastian.' Mostly truthful. Mostly flattering. You write your novel's protagonist into the bio. Within an hour, three messages. To choose “Reply to the first carefully” means meeting The First Client; “Reply to a safer-seeming one” sends you toward Helen, the Editor instead.

choices.consequence: You choose to reply to the first carefully. It opens the route to The First Client, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.
You reply to a safer-seeming one. The decision moves you toward Helen, the Editor and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: A man in his fifties, polite, nervous. He talks about his ex-wife. You take, mentally, the smallest possible notes. He pays in cash. He thanks you. You walk home with seventy pounds and a stomach that has not decided how it feels.

choices.consequence: Capitalize on the rawness. You commit to write the scene tonight. By Your Day Job, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.
You commit to wait a week before writing. By The Client Who Reads, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: Your literary agent, Helen, calls. She wants to know what you're working on. You tell her the truth in a careful sentence. She is silent. Then she says, 'Be careful. Be specific. The distance between Your Day Job and The Client Who Reads begins with the choice between “Send Helen a chapter immediately” and “Keep Helen in the dark for the first draft.”

choices.consequence: Make her your sounding board. You choose to send Helen a chapter immediately. It opens the route to Your Day Job, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

choices.text: Keep Helen in the dark for the first draft
choices.consequence: You choose to keep Helen in the dark for the first draft. It opens the route to The Client Who Reads, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: You are also, technically, a junior writer at a magazine. Your colleague Amna notices you have been very tired. She asks if you are okay. You say yes. You say it slightly too quickly. Choose “Tell Amna the truth” and Helen's Concern comes into view; choose “Tell her you're just sleep-deprived” and the road bends toward The Borderline Night.

choices.consequence: You tell Amna the truth. The decision moves you toward Helen's Concern and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.
You tell her you're just sleep-deprived. The decision moves you toward The Borderline Night and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: A regular — an academic in his sixties — recognizes your debut short story collection. 'You're him,' he says, gently. 'I thought so.' He pays anyway. He recommends a book on Foucault. You read it. You don't know what to do with the information.

choices.text: Use him as a long, careful conversation partner
choices.consequence: You choose to use him as a long, careful conversation partner. It opens the route to Helen's Concern, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

choices.text: Stop seeing him; the line is too thin
choices.consequence: You stop seeing him; the line is too thin. The decision moves you toward The Borderline Night and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: Helen, after reading two chapters, calls late. 'Two questions,' she says. 'One: is the work good? Yes. Two: are you?' You realize you don't have a different answer for each. “Tell her the answer is the same and you don't know” opens the route to Your Family. “Tell her you're fine — finish the book first” changes the terms and carries you toward The First Draft.

choices.text: Tell her the answer is the same and you don't know
choices.consequence: You tell her the answer is the same and you don't know. The decision moves you toward Your Family and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

choices.text: Tell her you're fine — finish the book first
choices.consequence: You tell her you're fine — finish the book first. The decision moves you toward The First Draft and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: A booking goes slightly wrong — nothing dangerous, just unsettling. You go home with a feeling you don't want in your notes. You sit on the kitchen floor with the lights off for an hour. “Take a week off” opens the route to Your Family. “Write the unsettling scene with full honesty” changes the terms and carries you toward The First Draft.

choices.consequence: You choose to take a week off. It opens the route to Your Family, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

choices.text: Write the unsettling scene with full honesty
choices.consequence: You commit to write the unsettling scene with full honesty. By The First Draft, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: You go home to Brighton for a weekend. Your mother makes Sunday roast. You realize you have not lied to her about the specifics, only the substance. You realize you'd prefer not to lie at all.

choices.consequence: You choose to tell her the truth gently. It opens the route to The Bidding War, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

choices.text: Wait until the book is out
choices.consequence: You commit to wait until the book is out. By The Decision, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: You finish the first draft on a Wednesday at 3 a.m. You realize, reading it, that the novel is good and is also a kind of exposure. The book is, you slowly understand, going to make you a public person whether or not you choose to be.

choices.text: Send the draft to Helen the next morning
choices.consequence: You send the draft to Helen the next morning. The decision moves you toward The Bidding War and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

choices.text: Sit on the draft for a month first
choices.consequence: You commit to sit on the draft for a month first. By The Decision, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: Helen sends the manuscript. Three publishers want it. The advance is, by a wide margin, the most money you have ever been offered for anything. The distance between The Publicity Tour and Your Family, Reading begins with the choice between “Accept the biggest offer” and “Accept the editor you think believes in the book most.”

choices.consequence: You choose to accept the biggest offer. It opens the route to The Publicity Tour, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

choices.text: Accept the editor you think believes in the book most
choices.consequence: You choose to accept the editor you think believes in the book most. It opens the route to Your Family, Reading, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: You sit with the question of whether to keep working as 'Sebastian' once the book is sold. You realize the answer is, finally, no. You realize you've been hoping the book would let you stop.

choices.consequence: You choose to stop the day after sale. It opens the route to The Publicity Tour, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.
You taper off for a month. The decision moves you toward Your Family, Reading and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: Pubs ask you the same questions — autobiographical, ethics, exploitation. You answer the same answer with growing patience: the book is a novel. It is also, you admit, a kind of field notes. The paths divide here: “Be plain about the field notes” leads into The Long Profile, while “Lean into the novelist's distance” makes Amna's Question the next reckoning.

choices.text: Be plain about the field notes
choices.consequence: You commit to be plain about the field notes. By The Long Profile, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.
You choose to lean into the novelist's distance. It opens the route to Amna's Question, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: Your father reads the book in three days. He calls you. He says, 'Did you have to write the bath scene?' You laugh, because the laugh is also relief. He says, 'I'm proud of you.' He hangs up before you can answer.

choices.consequence: You call him back. The decision moves you toward The Long Profile and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

choices.text: Write him a letter the next morning
choices.consequence: You commit to write him a letter the next morning. By Amna's Question, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: A long magazine profile is, you decide, your chance to be honest in your own words. You spend three days with a reporter you trust. The profile, when it lands, is fair, generous, and slightly more vulnerable than you planned.

choices.text: Trust the profile and be done with the press
choices.consequence: You choose to trust the profile and be done with the press. It opens the route to Second Book, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

choices.text: Use it as a platform for sex worker rights advocacy
choices.consequence: You commit to use it as a platform for sex worker rights advocacy. By Brighton, Visiting, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: Amna, who has read the book, asks if you want to teach a workshop she runs for young writers from working-class backgrounds. You realize you can be useful in a way the book by itself doesn't manage.

choices.consequence: You choose to take the workshop. It opens the route to Second Book, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.
You choose to take a sabbatical first. It opens the route to Brighton, Visiting, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: Your second book is, mercifully, about something completely else. Helen jokes, kindly, that you have ten years to write any kind of book you want now. You realize that, more than the money, that is the gift.

choices.text: Write the book you've always quietly wanted to
choices.consequence: You choose to write the book you've always quietly wanted to. It opens the route to The Reading, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

choices.text: Write the book that helps the next 'Sebastian'
choices.consequence: You commit to write the book that helps the next 'Sebastian'. By The Reading, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: You go home more often. Your mother makes Sunday roast. Your father reads everything you publish, eventually, in his armchair. You realize, late, that your job was never the secret — it was just the symptom of being twenty-six and lonely. You are, slowly, less lonely.

choices.consequence: You choose to move back near them. It opens the route to The Honest Lunch, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.
You commit to stay in London, visit often. By The Honest Lunch, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: A bookshop in Bloomsbury asks you to read. The room is small and full. A young person in the second row, embarrassed, asks if they can speak to you after. You realize the reading is, also, an office hour.

choices.text: Stay an hour for the second-row reader
choices.consequence: You stay an hour for the second-row reader. The decision moves you toward The Shape of It and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.
You commit to be gracious and brief. By The Shape of It, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: Helen takes you to lunch and asks, plainly, what kind of writer you want to be in five years. You realize the answer has, finally, come into focus. The answer is, as Helen suspected it would be, both.

choices.consequence: You tell her the plan. The decision moves you toward The Shape of It and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

choices.text: Tell her you'll send it on paper
choices.consequence: You tell her you'll send it on paper. The decision moves you toward The Shape of It and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: You sit at your desk and write the next sentence. The sentence is yours. The pen is yours. The years ahead, surprisingly, are also yours. You choose which kind of writer you're going to be.

choices.consequence: You commit to the career writer. By A Long Career, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.
Shorter shelf, more readers helped. You commit to the writer-teacher. By The Workshop, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.
You choose to the Brighton writer. It opens the route to Brighton, Eventually, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: You write books for the next thirty years. Some are good. Some are very good. Your first is the one that everyone asks about, still, even after the others have outsold it. You answer the same way: it was a beginning. You have learned to mean that.

Your second book is a quiet, careful guide to writing through difficult life material. It is recommended in three different MFA programs. You teach two workshops a year. You realize, surprised, that you are good at it.

You move back. You buy a small flat with a view of the sea. You write, you visit your parents, you walk the pier in the rain. The novel becomes, in time, a thing you wrote — not a thing you are. That distinction, you realize, is the whole project.
